title: Could Have Been Better. Could Have Been Worse
summary:
Could Have Been Better. Could Have Been Worse 

             
             
            If the bond market was a Mario Bro, it found a gold star at some point on Wednesday. As Thursday afternoon, the gold star ran out of juice and we're back to regular old Mario. In other words, astonishing resilience/bullishness has been replaced by a sideways-to-slightly-weaker grind. It could be as simple as the desire among traders to consolidate recent gains without getting too carried away. Ongoing selling in tech stocks ostensibly allowed for another bond rally, so the fact that we lost a bit of ground could end up looking like an important clue about resistance. A mid-day spike in oil prices may have added just a bit of upward pressure in yields, but it's more likely correlation>causation as oil has been higher all week. Losses were minimal as of 3pm, leaving most of the week's rally intact.

title: Existing Home Sales Treading Same Old Water
summary: If you're busy, we can make this quick. Existing home sales dropped sharply from over 6m units per year starting in 2022 and had bottomed out around 4m units per year by the end of 2023. They've done essentially nothing exciting since then and the latest update is no exception. The end.     If you prefer to read an article-sized article, here you go:  Existing-home sales edged higher in September with The National Association of REALTORS® reporting a  1.5% increase  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  3.99 million . August and September mark the two slowest months for home sales this year, as higher borrowing costs continued to limit the pool of qualified buyers.  “Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home,” Yun said. Freddie Mac's average 30-year fixed rate climbed to  6.86% in September , up from 6.67% in August and 6.35% a year earlier.  Inventory continued to offer buyers more options than they had a year ago, although the latest increase was relatively modest. Total housing inventory reached  1.60 million units , up  1.9% from August  and  4.6% year over year .  Buyers may also have more room to negotiate as homes take longer to sell. The median time on market increased to  33 days , up from 31 days in August. Yun said the combination of higher inventory and longer selling times could require sellers to offer price reductions or other incentives to attract buyers.

title: Only a Modest Decline For Mortgage Apps. Next Week Should Improve
summary:
Mortgage applications continued to lose ground as mortgage rates held near their highest levels in nearly three years. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  2.7% decline  in total mortgage application volume for the week ending October 9.  That's an important date, because a substantial majority of a fairly sharp decline in interest rates occurred AFTER October 9. As such, next week's data is a great opportunity to see the impact of lower rates.   Purchase activity took another step back, with the seasonally adjusted Purchase Index falling  4%  for the week and running  16% below year-ago levels . Refinances were nearly unchanged, slipping just 0.4%, but remained  56% lower  than a year earlier.  The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate edged up to  7.50% , its highest level since November 2023 and more than a percentage point above its level a year ago. MBA's Joel Kan notes,  “As a result, borrowers continue to rely more on ARM loans to help lower their monthly payments."   ARMs accounted for  10.5% of all applications , the highest share since October 2025. The refinance share also ticked higher, reaching 37.7% of total applications from 37.0% the previous week, with a 5% drop in FHA refinance applications being the main driver of the small overall decline. title: Mortgage Rates Slightly Higher Today, But Sharply Lower This Week
summary: After dropping sharply over the past 5 days, mortgage rates finally reminded us that they're still capable of moving higher. Thankfully, today's bump was modest in the recent context, only adding 0.04% to a 30yr fixed that had fallen 0.27% since October 7th.   Even though today's losses were minimal, they're potentially informative. Much of this week's improvement can be traced to concerns surrounding tech companies, and possible warning signs about a reduction in AI-related spending/investment throughout the sector.   While it's too early to draw any conclusions about such things, we can certainly observe a strong correlation between tech stocks and interest rates as of October 8th. What's notable about today is that rates refused to follow tech stocks any lower, even though the NASDAQ had an even worse day than it did on Wednesday.   The counterpoint--if there is one--is that oil prices launched higher, which may have prevented bonds/rates from getting too excited. Still, oil has been moving higher during the same time frame that rates have been improving, so one could easily ask "why does oil suddenly matter now?" There's not really a great answer to that question, so we're left to conclude that bonds/rates are feeling a bit of resistance after this week's bull run.

title: AI Document, Broker, U/W, QC Tools; Lender/Investor Earnings; Credit News; LO Retention Examined
summary: The MBA believes that 2027’s production will be 5 percent less than 2026’s and be below $2 trillion. “Rob, are you hearing that, with volumes down (units and volume), lenders are once again examining keeping entire loan originator workforces?” Indeed I am. At the most basic level, as we move through autumn and into winter with no sign of greatly improved rates and the spring “home buying season” five months away, lenders are asking, “Is the LO carrying him/herself?” Lenders are moving LOs to part-time status, cutting benefits when possible, or suggesting they “find success elsewhere.” Many are shifting. RETR reports that from January through September 9, 2026, independent mortgage bankers lost roughly 100 net loan officers, representing approximately $1.8 billion in production, while the non-delegated, broker and wholesale channels gained 327 net loan officers and nearly $7 billion in production. Technology-enabled platforms make it easier to move production into operating models with lower costs and more efficient fulfillment. (Today’s podcast can be found here. This week’s ‘casts are presented by nCino, the platform for agentic AI in mortgage lending. nCino is helping mortgage lenders deliver a faster, simpler path to homeownership. Today’s has an interview with SF Realtor Arrian Binnings on how real estate agents and mortgage originators build effective partnerships and how AI may change their work.) title: Bonds Still Capable of Selling
summary: The past two days saw a unique confluence of factors that led to a precipitous, unexpected, and fairly large rally in the bond market. The easiest scapegoat is the general notion of fear surrounding AI/tech share prices and debt contagion. One simple effect was investors reallocating out of stocks and into bonds. Another effect could be investors shifting out of AI corporate debt into safer havens. Either way, it doesn't feel like a coincidence that tech stocks slid roughly 5% over the exact same time frame as the 10yr rallied from 5.34 to 5.07. If we use the QQQ ETF as a loose benchmark for tech, today isn't great, but it's better than yesterday's lows. The flood of short-covering and value buying in bonds has run its course and there would need to be fresh motivations for additional gains--either from a renewed tech rout or troublingly weak economic data. None of today's reports are remotely important enough for that, so unless tech tanks hard, we wouldn't expect the rally to extend. Modest weakness in the AM is entirely forgivable and perhaps even reassuring. In other words, we could have imagined a sharper pull-back on a morning like this. If bonds end up rallying more than is justified by other inputs, it would be a positive indication for bigger-picture trend shift potential.
